newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - S.Africa's call to arms - By Tony Twine.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - S.Africa's call to arms - By Tony Twine.

text.p: By Tony Twine, an economist at Econometrix financial consultancy
The South African economy has, in the statistical description of its composition, several odd looking imbalances in the contributions of various sectors and industries to its economic aggregates.

For instance, the mining sector contributes only about eight percent of the gross domestic product, but that eight percent provides the lion's share of the country's exports - nearly 50 percent, depending on global prices and the physical demand for minerals.

There is very little beneficiation of the considerable mineral output of the country, a strategic weakness which will take time and sizeable capital investments to overcome, but which provides a sensible avenue for a rapid increase in the value added in South Africa.

This inequality between the share of production and the share of export value is so large that it obviously impacts on the comparative shares of other sectors in the economy. For instance, virtually one quarter of GDP comes from the manufacturing sector, but it contributes substantially less to the value exports.

There are strong historic reasons for this particular imbalance - during the years of increasing isolation, which can be traced back to the 1960s, South African industry was oriented almost entirely towards import displacement, just in case a sanctions stranglehold on any strategic product or groups of products really began to bite. The heritage of those inward oriented years is still with South Africa seven years after the first steps down the long road to political normalisation.

Even during the 1960s, one of the few embargoes which did begin to bite at a strategic level was that of arms exports to South Africa. During the second half of that decade, the country's major military equipment was mainly west European in origin. The standard army rifle was the NATO, FN (Belgian), French Mirage 111, CZ Interceptors flew along side British made Vampires and Canberra bombers. North American Sabre fighters, veterans of the Korean War, were in the last years of service, while the DC 3 Dokota was still the standard military transport, augmented by the new arrivals of C130 Hercules transporters. The standard APC was the British Saracen, while a handful of Frigates (ex Royal Navy destroyers, converted for anti-submarine warfare) and three French Daphne class submarines provided seaward defence. Communication and detection equipment all had origins familiar to the military in the western world.

We all know how that changed over the next 25 years. From virtually nothing, the South African arms industry - perhaps it would be better to use the more current buzz phrase, Defence Industry - has grown into one of the top ten in the world. What it lacks in mass production capacity is balanced by the wide variety of military hardware which it offers. For obvious reasons, not much was broadcast about the industry during the laager mentality years, and there was little given away in the form of exports of know how and techniques. But, with no apparent enemy on the horizon, that game has changed over the past seven years and, much to the chagrin of other global players in the international defence industry, South Africa has emerged as an exporter of note.

What seens to have upset the global military powers has been the countries with which South Africa has come within striking distance of concluding arms deals. In the headlines over the past year have been Syria (tank firing control systems), Iraq (a bed for tank turrets) and China (radar systems). Middle eastern countries which would have previously been supplied out of the arms arsenal of the Soviet Union must all be looking for alternative sources of military hardware. They are not likely to be able to buy from America or its NATO allies, so why not South Africa.

A National Party spokesman, who presumably knows what he is talking about, last week pointed to the fact that the arms industry is South Africas' single largest exporter of manufactured goods. Once again, this is one of those proportional imbalances to be found in South Africa's economy. Insiders say that the defence industry is made up of abut 700 individual companies, the majority of which are quite tiny. Its value and volume of production is certainly not in the class of domestic industrial giants like the chemical and motor industries, but it enjoys a disproportionately large share of manufactured exports.

Political and diplomatic pressure, couched in terms of morality, is already being exerted on South Africa to select its arms export agreements with greater discretion. But it is arguable whether there is any morality in arms manufacturing or trading whatsoever. Some may go so far as to say that it is totally immoral business, but the term amoral offers itself as a less prejudicial and realistic alternative. If South Africa does not supply, somebody else will, possible illicitly. The U.S., whose legal system apparently attempts to entrench their questionable moral high ground on dealing with arms to Middle eastern countries in particular, does not have a proud record of containing arms supplies themselves. Just ask Oliver North. Apart from reports that there were three European countries also bidding for the Syria tank system deal, yet another crept out of the woodwork just as the fuss was cooling down between the U.S. State Department and South Africa.
